trace.detail: section through the building on a plane perpendicular to the street: pavement to eaves at 14.918 m up the facade plane, then the brisis ON the diagonal_45 envelope to the fold 1.914 m above the eaves, then the terrasson to a ridge 3.200 m above them and 7.964 m back from the facade — 5 point(s). The brisis is not chosen: it is the boundary of the legal solid, sampled, because a builder takes every centimetre of garret floor the law allows. What stands above it IS chosen — it is a roof, not an envelope (A8.3) — and it is inscribed inside the same boundary.

the fold is at 1.914 m over the eaves, 59.8% of the comble, and 1.914 m back from the facade — where the terrasson, arriving at the ridge 7.964 m back, meets the diagonal_45 envelope on its way down (A12.1). It is NOT the 2.900 m the garret's own wall stands: that number is a count of whole chambres de bonne and it puts the fold within 0.300 m of the ridge, leaving a hairline terrasson and a flat deck across the rest of the plot — a slab with a nick near the top rather than a comble brisé. The section is over-determined once the terrasson's pitch is fixed, so the SAME three numbers are read as a terrasson running the whole way to the ridge and a fold wherever that line crosses the gabarit. The ridge did not move (3.200 m, the decree's and the measured plates'); only the fold did, and it slid down the envelope, so it is still a point setback_at returned.

the comble springs from the eaves the building actually has (14.918 m, the sum of its storeys), not from the legal cornice ceiling (17.55 m) — the diagonal springs from the égout du toit, so a building that stopped short of its ceiling carries the whole roof SHAPE down with it. Its CEILING does not come down with it: 2.633 m of cornice height went unbuilt, and that is legal space the building declined to occupy rather than space it forfeited, so the SAME curve is traced to a taller top and the comble MAY stand 5.833 m over these eaves — 2.633 m more than the 3.200 m the ridge stands over the cornice — on a parcel with 9.000 m to give. The springing did not move; only the top did (A3.1). It does NOT stand there: a ceiling is not a height, and building to it made the roof grow by exactly what the stone gave up, so every immeuble in Paris came out at its legal total (A8.5). What was built is 3.200 m — the garret storeys behind the brisis and the terrasson closing over them — set back 7.964 m, leaving 2.633 m of legal volume nobody had a use for. This silhouette is inscribed below the envelope sprung from its own eaves (worst margin -0.000 m); measured from the legal cornice — the weaker line, which is not the test — it would be +0.000 m. A margin of exactly zero is the facade standing on the street line, which is where a Paris facade stands.
